items.key: being you: a new science of consciousness
items.text: The author's own earlier book is cited as containing the fuller argument for why life may matter for consciousness.
items.context: Being You: A New Science of Consciousness

items.key: frankenstein
items.text: Used as a cultural touchstone for the long, mostly unhappy history of stories about synthetic minds.
items.context: Frankenstein

items.key: 2001: a space odyssey
items.text: HAL 9000 is cited as a cultural example of a synthetic mind story that ends badly for humans.
items.context: 2001: A Space Odyssey

items.key: ex machina
items.text: Used repeatedly, including for the 'Garland test' idea, to explore what convinces humans a machine is conscious.
items.context: Ex Machina

items.key: klara and the sun
items.text: Cited as another cultural example of a story about an artificial mind that thinks and feels.
items.context: Klara and the Sun

items.key: interview in the washington post claiming lamda is conscious
items.text: Cited as an early, controversial claim that a chatbot is conscious, which the essay argues against.
items.context: Interview in The Washington Post claiming LaMDA is conscious

items.key: views on machine consciousness (interviews/statements)
items.text: Chalmers's claim that conscious machines may soon be possible, and his neural-replacement thought experiment, are both examined and challenged.
items.context: Views on machine consciousness (interviews/statements)

items.key: statements claiming ai systems are already conscious
items.text: Hinton's claim that conscious machines already exist, and his 'mortal computation' idea, are both discussed and disputed.
items.context: Statements claiming AI systems are already conscious

items.key: article on the need to take ai welfare seriously
items.text: Cited as evidence that serious thinkers are pushing to treat AI systems as moral patients, a claim the essay questions.
items.context: Article on the need to take AI welfare seriously

items.key: what is it like to be a bat?
items.text: Nagel's definition of consciousness as 'something it is like to be' an organism frames the essay's core distinction between consciousness and intelligence.
items.context: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?

items.key: more everything forever
items.text: Its idea of pareidolia is used to describe why people wrongly see consciousness in AI, likened to seeing faces in random patterns.
items.context: More Everything Forever

items.key: foundational work defining the universal turing machine and computation
items.text: Turing's formal definition of computation underlies the 'computational functionalism' assumption the essay argues against.
items.context: Foundational work defining the universal Turing machine and computation

items.key: a logical calculus of the ideas immanent in nervous activity
items.text: Their landmark paper showing simplified neuron networks can do logical operations underlies the brain-as-computer metaphor the essay challenges.
items.context: A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity

items.key: work showing neural networks with memory are turing complete
items.text: Kleene's demonstration that simple neuron networks with memory can implement any algorithm supports the (later challenged) brain-as-computer view.
items.context: Work showing neural networks with memory are Turing complete

items.key: research on neurons spiking to clear metabolic waste
items.text: Their finding that some neurons fire mainly to clear waste products is used to show a silicon copy could never perfectly replace a biological neuron.
items.context: Research on neurons spiking to clear metabolic waste

items.key: example of the watt governor as a non-computational system
items.text: Van Gelder's steam-engine governor example is used to argue that not all functional systems are best understood as computational.
items.context: Example of the Watt governor as a non-computational system

items.key: biological naturalism (view that life is necessary for consciousness)
items.text: Searle's idea that biological properties are necessary for consciousness is the basis for the essay's 'life matters' argument.
items.context: Biological naturalism (view that life is necessary for consciousness)

items.key: recent research paper on life and consciousness
items.text: A research paper by the author is cited alongside the book as fuller support for the life-consciousness connection.
items.context: Recent research paper on life and consciousness

items.key: are you living in a computer simulation?
items.text: Bostrom's simulation hypothesis is examined and criticized for assuming, without argument, that a running computer program would be conscious.
items.context: Are You Living in a Computer Simulation?

items.key: lectures on ethics
items.text: Kant's argument that treating seemingly-feeling things as feelingless is psychologically harmful supports the essay's point about conscious-seeming AI.
items.context: Lectures on Ethics

items.key: public warnings about the dangers of conscious-seeming ai
items.text: Cited as leading AI figures who have begun to flag the risks posed by AI that merely seems conscious.
items.context: Public warnings about the dangers of conscious-seeming AI

items.key: description of ai as a mirror reflecting our digitized past
items.text: Vallor's metaphor of AI as a mirror supports the essay's closing point that we see ourselves reflected in, and mistaken for, our algorithms.
items.context: Description of AI as a mirror reflecting our digitized past

items.key: quote on technology making us forget what we know about life
items.text: Turkle's remark closes the essay, reinforcing the warning against forgetting the difference between living and artificial minds.
items.context: Quote on technology making us forget what we know about life
